passages.source_text: οὐχ ἄλλως δὲ τὸ πολὺ τῆς σπουδῆς πρὸς κάθαρσιν ὑμῶν ἀναδέξασθαι ὑπομενεῖτε, ἐὰν μήγε αὐτοῖς ὀργισθέντες ἐπιπλήξητε περὶ ὧν ὡς ἀχρεῖοι δοῦλοι ἐνηδρεύθητε συνθέμενοι ταῖς κακαῖς ὑμῶν ἐπιθυμίαις, ἵνα τὴν δικαίαν ὑμῶν ὀργὴν τῷ νῷ ὡς πῦρ χερσευσάσῃ ἀρούρῃ ἐπαφεῖναι δυνηθῆτε. εἰ μὲν οὖν οὐκ ἔχετε δίκαιον πῦρ (τὴν κατὰ τῶν κακῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν ὀργὴν λέγω), μάθετε ἀπὸ ποίων καλῶν ἐνηδρεύθητε καὶ πρὸς ποίαν κόλασιν κατηρτίσθητε καὶ ὑπὸ τίνος ἠπατήθητε, καὶ οὕτως ὑμῶν ὁ νοῦς νήψας καὶ ὥσπερ πῦρ ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ πέμψαντος ἡμᾶς διδασκαλίας ἐξαφθεὶς εἰς ὀργήν, τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ. πιστεύσατέ μοι. ὅτι θελήσαντες πάντα κατορθῶσαι δυνήσεσθε.

ἀλλὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἔδει ποιῆσαι ἡμᾶς μηδὲ ὅλως περὶ τοιούτων ἐνθυμεῖσθαι. ταῦτα λέγοντες ἀγνοεῖτε τί ἐστιν τὸ αὐτεξούσιον, καὶ πῶς δυνατὸν ἐστιν ἀγαθοὺς τῷ ὄντι εἶναι. ὅτι ὁ ἰδίᾳ προαιρέσει ὢν ἀγαθὸς ὄντως ἀγαθός ἐστιν, ὁ δὲ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου ἀνάγκης ἀγαθὸς γενόμενος ὄντως οὐκ ἔστιν, ὅτι μὴ ἰδίᾳ προαιρέσει ἐστὶν ὅ ἐστιν. ἐπεὶ οὖν τὸ ἑκάστου ἐλεύθερον ἀποτελεῖ τὸ ὄντως ἀγαθὸν καὶ δεικνύει τὸ ὄντως κακόν, ἐν ἑκάστῳ γενέσθαι ἐχθρὸν ἢ φίλον διὰ τῶν ὑποθέσεων ὁ θεὸς ἐμηχανήσατο. οὒ φησιν, ἀλλὰ πᾶν ὃ ἐνθυμούμεθα, αὐτὸς ἡμᾶς ποιεῖ νοεῖν. παύσασθε· τί πλεῖον βλασφημεῖτε οἱ τοῦτο λέγοντες; εἰ γὰρ πᾶν ὅ,τι ἂν ἐνθυμηθῶμεν, ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐνεργούμεθα, αὐτὸν αἴτιον λέγετε πορνειῶν, ἀσελγειῶν, πλεονεξιῶν καὶ πάσης βλασφημίας. παύσασθε δυσφημοῦντες, οἱ εὐφημεῖν καὶ πᾶσαν τιμὴν αὐτῷ ἀπονέμειν ὀφείλοντες. καὶ μὴ λέγετε Οὐκ ἐπιδικάζεται ὁ θεὸς τιμῆς. εἰ γὰρ αὐτὸς οὐδενὸς ἐπιδικάζεται, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε ἡμᾶς ἐχρῆν εἰς τὸ δίκαιον ἀφορῶντας τὸν ἐν πᾶσιν ἡμᾶς εὐεργετήσαντα εὐχαρίστῳ ἀμείψασθαι φωνῇ.

κἂν γὰρ τῇ τοῦ σώματος λύσει τὴν κόλασιν ἐκφύγητε, πῶς τὴν ψυχὴν ὑμῶν ἄφθαρτον οὖσαν διὰ τῆς φθορᾶς φυγεῖν δυνήσεσθε; ἀθάνατος γὰρ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τῶν ἀσεβῶν, οἷς ἄμεινον ἦν μὴ ἄφθαρτον αὐτὴν ἔχειν. κολαζομένη γὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀσβέστου πυρὸς ἀπεράντῳ τιμωρίᾳ καὶ μὴ θνήσκουσα, ἐπὶ κακῷ τῷ αὐτῆς τέλος λαβεῖν οὐκ ἔχει. ἀλλ’ ἴσως ἐρεῖ τις ὑμῶν Φοβεῖς ἡμᾶς, Πέτρε. διδάξατε οὖν ἡμᾶς πῶς σιγῶντες ἐροῦμεν τὰ ὄντα ὡς ἔστιν· ἄλλως γὰρ αὐτὰ ὑμῖν σημαίνειν οὐ δυνάμεθα. ἐάν τε σιγήσωμεν, ἐνεδρεύεσθε ὑπὸ τῶν κακῶν διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν — ἐάν τε λαλήσωμεν, ὡς ἐπὶ ψευδεῖ ὑποθέσει φοβοῦντες ὑμᾶς ὑποπτευόμεθα. πῶς οὖν ἐτάσωμεν τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι καὶ πανούργως ὑποσπείροντι ὑμῖν τὰς θεῷ ἐχθραινούσας ὑπονοίας προφάσει τῆς πρὸς θεὸν φιλίας; διαλλάγητε ἑαυτοῖς· ὑπὲρ γὰρ τῆς ὑμῶν σωτηρίας γίνεται ἡ μετὰ εὐποιΐας πρὸς αὐτὸν καταφυγή. ἔχθρα τις ἐστὶν θεῷ ἐν ὑμῖν ἄλογος ἐπιθυμία· ὑπονοίᾳ γὰρ φρονήσεως τὴν ἄγνοιαν κρατύνει.

ἄλλοι δὲ λέγουσιν Οὐ πεφρόντικεν ἡμῶν ὁ θεός. καὶ τοῦτο ψεῦδός ἐστιν. εἰ γὰρ ὄντως οὐκ ἐφρόντιζεν, οὐκ ἂν οὐδὲ τὸν ἥλιον αὐτοῦ ἀνέτελλεν ἐπὶ ἀγαθοὺς καὶ πονηροὺς οὔτε τὸν ὑετὸν αὐτοῦ ἔφερεν ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους. ἕτεροι δὲ λέγουσιν Εὐσεβέστεροί ἐσμεν καὶ αὐτὸν καὶ τὰ ἀγάλματα σέβοντες. οὐκ οἶμαι, εἰ τοῦτο λέγων τις ἐρεῖ βασιλεῖ Τὴν ἴσην σοι ἀπονέμω τιμήν, οἵαν καὶ τοῖς νεκροῖς καὶ τῇ ἐρριμμένῃ κοπρίᾳ· οὐκ οἴομαι εἰ καλῶς ἀπαλλάξει. ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις Κοπρίαν λέγεις τὰ σεβάσματα ἡμῶν; ναί φημι. ἄχρηστα γὰρ ὑμῖν αὐτὰ ἐποιήσατε, εἰς τὸ σέβειν καταριθμήσαντες, τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν ἴσως εἰς ἄλλο τι (εἰς χρῆσιν κόπρου) εὐχρηστησάσης. νῦν δὲ οὐδὲ εἰς τοῦτο χρησιμεύει, ὅτε μετασχηματίσαντες προσκυνεῖτε. πῶς δὲ καὶ εὐσεβέστεροι εἶναί φατε οἱ πάντων ἀσεβέστατοι; ταύτῃ αὐτῇ τῇ μιᾷ καὶ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀμαρτίᾳ ψυχῆς ὄλεθρον ὀφείλοντες τὰ ἀληθῆ, ἐὰν ἐπιμείνητε. ὡς γὰρ εἴ τις υἱὸς πολλὰ εὐεργετούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς ἑτέρῳ τινὶ τῷ μὴ πατρὶ τὴν ὀφειλομένην τῷ πατρὶ ἀποδῴη τιμήν, πάντως ἀποκληρονόμος γίνεται· ἐπὰν δὲ κατὰ γνώμην τοῦ πατρὸς βιοὺς εὐχαριστῇ ἐπὶ ταῖς εὐεργεσίαις, εὐλόγως κληρονόμος γίνεται.

ἄλλοι δὲ λέγουσιν Ἀσεβεῖν μέλλομεν, ἐὰν τὰ παραδοθέντα ἡμῖν ἐκ πατέρων σεβάσματα καταλείψωμεν· ὅμοιον γὰρ ἐστὶν τῷ παραθήκην φυλάξαι. οὐκοῦν τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ κἂν λῃστοῦ τις ἢ πατρὸς ἢ αἰσχροβίου, οὐκ ὀφείλει ὁ υἱὸς νήψας τὸ κρεῖττον ἑλέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἀσεβήσῃ καὶ μὴ τὰ ἴσα τοῖς γονεῦσιν ποιῶν ἀμαρτάνῃ; πῶς δὲ ἀνόητοι οἱ λέγοντες Ταῦτα προσκυνοῦμεν, ἵνα μὴ αὐτῷ ὀχλῶμεν; ὡς ὀχλουμένου θεοῦ ἐφ’ οἷς εὐφημεῖται, μὴ ὀχλουμένου δὲ ἐφ’ οἷς ἀχαριστούμενος βλασφημεῖται. διὰ τί οὖν, ὁπόταν ἐποχὴ ὑετοῦ γένηται, πρὸς οὐρανὸν τὰ πάντα ἀφορῶντες εὐχὰς καὶ λιτὰς ἀπονέμετε; καὶ ὅταν ἐπιτύχητε, τάχιον ἐπιλανθάνεσθε; ἀμήσαντες γὰρ ἢ τρυγήσαντες εὐθέως τοῖς μηδὲν οὖσιν εἰδώλοις τὰς ἀπαρχὰς ἀπονέμετε, τάχιον ἐπιλανθανόμενοι τοῦ εὐεργετήσαντος θεοῦ. καὶ οὕτως εἰς ἄλση καὶ εἰς τοὺς ναοὺς γενόμενοι θυσίας ἐπιτελοῦντες εὐωχεῖσθε. διὰ τοῦτο οἱ μὲν ὑμῶν λέγουσιν Παρηγορίας καὶ τοῦ εὐωχεῖσθαι χάριν καλῶς ταῦτα ἐπινενοήται.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: You will not otherwise endure undertaking the great effort needed for your cleansing unless you become angry with yourselves and rebuke yourselves for the ways in which, like useless servants, you were ambushed by agreeing with your evil desires. Then you will be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated. So if you do not have righteous fire—I mean anger against evil desires—learn what good things you have been ambushed and deprived of, what punishment you have been prepared for, and by whom you have been deceived. In this way your mind, becoming clear-minded and kindled to anger like fire by the teaching of the one who sent us, may be able to consume the things that are against desire. Believe me: if you are willing, you will be able to set everything right.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB servant gloss; the comparison retains the underlying bonded-status and master-accountability sense of δοῦλοι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: may be able to consume the things that are against desire.
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ substantivizes the following prepositional phrase, and κατά with the supplied genitive τῆς naturally means against. The formal grouping preserves that syntax without silently replacing the genitive with an accusative or moving opposition to qualify the consuming action. Its precise intended sense remains difficult in the surrounding fire-and-desire argument; things belonging to desire would require a textual or syntactic account not established by this wording.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
source_issues.issue: The formal grouping the things that are against desire is defensible from the supplied article and genitive construction, but its fit with the surrounding fire-and-desire argument is difficult. This translation does not claim to resolve that difficulty or emend the Greek. The previous adverbial attachment is not retained, because an independent object for τὰ was not adequately established.

passages.text: “But from the beginning he ought to have made us not even think about such things at all.” In saying this, you do not know what freedom of choice is or how it is possible to be truly good. For the person who is good by his own choice is truly good; the person made good by someone else’s compulsion is not truly so, because he is not what he is by his own choice. Since each person’s freedom produces what is truly good and reveals what is truly evil, God has arranged, through the circumstances, for becoming an enemy or a friend to lie within each person. “No,” someone says, “rather, he himself makes us think everything that we think.” Stop! What further blasphemy are you speaking when you say this? For if, in everything we may think, we are moved by him, you are calling him the cause of sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed, and every blasphemy. Stop speaking ill of him, you who ought to speak well of him and assign him every honor. And do not say, “God does not claim honor.” Even if he claims nothing, we still ought, with an eye to what is just, to repay with a thankful voice the one who has benefited us in every way.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally self-determination or being in one’s own power; the paragraph explicitly contrasts personal choice and external compulsion.
ὑποθέσεις can denote situations, underlying conditions, or proposed matters; circumstances fits the arrangements in which choice operates without specifying their exact mechanism.
Preserves distinct vice categories without embellishing sexual content or reducing all three to a generic evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ γὰρ πᾶν ὅ,τι ἂν ἐνθυμηθῶμεν, ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐνεργούμεθα
lexical_decisions.chosen: For if, in everything we may think, we are moved by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: We remains the subject of ἐνεργούμεθα. Moved or actuated concerns the alleged divine agency in our thinking; it does not make thoughts into actions implemented by God.

passages.text: For even if you escape punishment through the dissolution of the body, how will you be able through destruction to escape your soul, which is indestructible? For even the soul of the impious is immortal; it would have been better for them not to have it indestructible. Punished by unquenchable fire with unending punishment and not dying, it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt. But perhaps one of you will say, “You frighten us, Peter.” Then teach us how we are to state things as they are while remaining silent, for we cannot make them known to you otherwise. If we remain silent, you are ambushed by evils through ignorance; if we speak, we are suspected of frightening you on a false premise. How, then, are we to deal with the evil lurking within you and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God under the pretext of friendship with God? Be reconciled with yourselves: taking refuge in him with good deeds is for your salvation. There is within you an irrational desire hostile to God; for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive phrase τὴν ὑμετέραν has no expressed feminine noun in the supplied wording. Within you preserves the contextual location of the lurking evil without inventing a named organ or restoring Greek words.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ κακῷ τῷ αὐτῆς τέλος λαβεῖν οὐκ ἔχει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains endless survival as harmful to the punished soul; the author’s claim is not harmonized with annihilation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ πανούργως ὑποσπείροντι ὑμῖν τὰς θεῷ ἐχθραινούσας ὑπονοίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: In you explicitly preserves ὑμῖν as the recipients of the sowing, separately from the earlier location of the lurking evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπονοίᾳ γὰρ φρονήσεως τὴν ἄγνοιαν κρατύνει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόνοια is a supposition, notion, or suspicion; supposed understanding preserves that cognitive claim rather than introducing a deliberate display or pretension. For retains the explanatory γάρ.

passages.text: Others say, “God has not cared about us.” This too is false. For if he truly did not care, he would not make his sun rise on good and evil people or send his rain on the righteous and unrighteous. Others say, “We are more reverent because we revere both him and the statues.” I do not think so—if someone who says this tells a king, “I assign you the same honor as I do the dead and discarded dung,” I do not think he will come off well. But someone will say, “Do you call our objects of reverence dung?” Yes, I say. For you made them useless to yourselves by counting them among objects of worship, although their substance might have served some other purpose, even the use of dung. But now it is not useful even for this, since you have reshaped it and worship it. How can you, the most impious of all, also claim to be more reverent? For this one incomparable sin alone you truly owe the destruction of your soul, if you persist. Just as a son who receives many benefits from his father and gives someone else, who is not his father, the honor owed to his father certainly becomes disinherited, so, when he lives according to his father’s judgment and gives thanks for the benefits, he reasonably becomes an heir.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν ἴσως εἰς ἄλλο τι (εἰς χρῆσιν κόπρου) εὐχρηστησάσης.
lexical_decisions.chosen: although their substance might have served some other purpose, even the use of dung
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the parenthetical comparison with useful dung rather than upgrading the idols into useful objects of worship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτῃ αὐτῇ τῇ μιᾷ καὶ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀμαρτίᾳ ψυχῆς ὄλεθρον ὀφείλοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: For this one incomparable sin alone you truly owe the destruction of your soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the severe stated consequence, with the following if-you-persist condition retained in the main text.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ οἶμαι, εἰ τοῦτο λέγων τις ἐρεῖ βασιλεῖ Τὴν ἴσην σοι ἀπονέμω τιμήν, οἵαν καὶ τοῖς νεκροῖς καὶ τῇ ἐρριμμένῃ κοπρίᾳ· οὐκ οἴομαι εἰ καλῶς ἀπαλλάξει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not think so—if ... I do not think he will come off well.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected edition repeats the negative assertion οὐκ οἶμαι / οὐκ οἴομαι around a conditional and syntactic restart. Both assertions remain, rather than being compressed into one; the restart is a supplied feature, not alleged OCR corruption.

passages.text: Others say, “We shall be acting impiously if we abandon the objects of reverence handed down to us from our fathers, for it is like keeping something entrusted to us.” By this reasoning, then, even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully, is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents? How senseless are those who say, “We worship these things so as not to trouble him himself,” as though God were troubled by being praised but not troubled by being blasphemed through ingratitude! Why, then, when rain is withheld, do you look to heaven for everything and offer prayers and entreaties? And when you succeed, why do you forget so quickly? For after reaping or gathering the vintage, you immediately assign the firstfruits to idols that are nothing, quickly forgetting the God who did you good. Then you go into sacred groves and temples and feast while performing sacrifices. For this reason some of you say, “These things have been well devised for comfort and feasting.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν λῃστοῦ τις ἢ πατρὸς ἢ αἰσχροβίου
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both printed ἢ disjunctions remain. The child relationship is inferred from the ensuing explicit son, not restored from missing text; the redundant father remains the supplied reading. Taking the first ἢ as conjectural ᾖ would create a smoother alternative, but that conjecture is not adopted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ὀφείλει ὁ υἱὸς νήψας τὸ κρεῖττον ἑλέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἀσεβήσῃ καὶ μὴ τὰ ἴσα τοῖς γονεῦσιν ποιῶν ἀμαρτάνῃ;
lexical_decisions.chosen: is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest ...?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Once clear-minded keeps νήψας circumstantial, not a second commanded action. Under by this reasoning, the question tests the proposed obligation to preserve ancestral practices and its consequence for choosing better. Is not obliged to choose is another rendering of οὐκ ὀφείλει; is not to choose makes the reductio consequence explicit without presenting it as Peter’s own counsel.

The neuter accusative τὰ πάντα qualifies the scope of looking, not the nominative people looking. Looking wholly toward heaven is another viable adverbial rendering; for everything is selected in the petition-for-rain context.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
